Chapter 11: Education and the Stories We Tell
You know, education is so much more than what happens in a classroom. It’s the stories we share at home, the lessons passed down from one generation to the next, and the images we see on screens or flip through in books.
These stories? They shape how we see ourselves and each other. They set the boundaries for what we believe is possible—and what we think is fair.
Picture a teacher, getting ready to teach American history. The textbook, of course, gives the standard version—heroes and triumphs, progress and freedom. But this teacher knows there’s always more beneath the surface. So, they dig deeper. They bring in fresh materials, invite guest speakers, and encourage their students to ask the tough questions.
Most folks don’t realize just how much the stories they hear shape their view of the world. If certain voices are left out, or if important histories are ignored, it becomes all too easy to accept inequality as just the way things are.
That’s why, for people who challenged these old, dominant stories, it became clear—education is a powerful tool for change. It can open minds, help us build empathy, and even spark action. But, if we’re not careful, it can just as easily reinforce old stereotypes and make injustice seem justified.
So, what does antiracism look like in education? It’s about searching for diverse perspectives, questioning what we’ve been told, and being willing to update those stories when we need to. It’s about making sure every student feels seen and valued—and not shying away from the tough truths.
And here’s the thing: this isn’t just the job of teachers. Parents, community leaders, even people who create media—all of us have a part to play. Because the stories we tell today? They’re shaping what’s possible for all of us tomorrow.
